<main class="site-main"><section class="page-intro"><p class="section-number">Note · Models and meaning</p><h1>Why PCA is useful intuition but not proof</h1><div class="article-meta"><span class="status">in bloom</span><span>updated 03 Jun 2026</span></div></section><article class="prose"><p>Principal component analysis is a good first flashlight. It compresses a high-dimensional cloud into directions that explain variance, which can make a structure easier to inspect.</p><p>It is not a proof that the visible structure is the structure that matters. A projection can hide separation, invent apparent clusters through scale choices, or make a convenient story look inevitable.</p><h2>The useful question</h2><p>Use the projection to generate a question: which variables, labels, or layers line up with this view? Then test that question in the original space, with a comparison that matches the claim.</p><blockquote>Pretty is a useful place to start. It is a poor place to stop.</blockquote><p>The limitation is not a reason to avoid PCA. It is a reason to keep the method attached to the question it helps you ask.</p></article></main>
